Two old booksellers

Saturday, 30 May, the Book Fair in the Retiro, a year after the launch in chapter 76. Doña Remedios has come from Seville, for the first time in her life, to sign with Ecaterina. Faustino is meeting her right now.
So you’re the bookseller from Triana. I was told you don’t mince your words.
And I was told you talk nineteen to the dozen. I see they hit the nail on the head.
Faustino, don’t pull her leg, she’s come all the way from Seville. She didn’t sleep a wink all night.
It’s true. I’m worn out. But here, among books, I’m in my element.
And is it true you kept a bookmark of Gil’s for sixty-eight years?
Yes, sir. And when Ecaterina told me the ending, I was stunned.
I knew Gil for forty years. He used to steal my customers. Did he steal yours too?
He never bought anything from me. He read for free on the floor. But now he’s sent me an author. We’re even.
Right, are you going to give me a hand with the boxes, or are you going to keep talking until closing time?
For me, carrying boxes is a piece of cake. Remedios, you sit down, today everything’s on me.

Idioms are said as one unit, like a single long word, with the main stress on the last element: «meter la PAta», «tomar el PElo», «no pegar Ojo».
The “d” and “b/v” between vowels are soft: CO-dos (almost “co-thos”), CLA-vo (a “v” without the teeth).
In Spain, “z” is pronounced [θ], like the English “th”: [peθ]. In Latin America: [pes].

Un año después

That year’s Madrid Book Fair began on the last Friday in May, as always, with the Retiro full of wooden stalls, readers in hats and children eating ice cream. Inés had got the publisher a stall of its own, number 112, and had decided that Ecaterina would sign there on the morning of Saturday the 30th. Saturday 30 May. It was exactly a year since Andrés had come into the marquee in his wheelchair and greeted the audience with an old-fashioned bookseller’s small gesture.

Ecaterina arrived in Madrid on Thursday, with Ana and Rosa Elena. This time she had brought neither a cast nor fear, just a small suitcase and an envelope with doña Remedios’s bookmark, which Andrei had photographed in April and which she had promised to return in person. But she wasn’t going to have to go to Seville. Inés had given her some news on the phone the week before: doña Remedios had agreed to come to Madrid to sign with her at the fair. She was eighty-four and hadn’t left Seville since 1974.

On Thursday evening, Ecaterina went alone to El Mostrador. She wanted to see the first copy before the fair began. It was still there, under the lamp, on the shelf at the back, with the cover facing the room. Lola told her that a little boy had tried to borrow it and his mother had explained, very seriously, that that book belonged to the bookseller. The boy had asked where the bookseller was. The mother hadn’t known what to answer. Lola had: she’d told him he was in all the books in the café, a little in each one. The boy had been stunned.

Doña Remedios arrived on Friday afternoon on the high-speed train, accompanied by her grandson, the guitar player, who was called Curro and had very precise instructions from his mother: that his grandmother shouldn’t get tired, that she should eat well and that she mustn’t get into any taxi without a seatbelt. Doña Remedios got off the train with a fan, a straw hat and a cloth bag full of books. She told Ecaterina you never travelled without books, just in case, and that at her age every trip could be the last, so you had to travel in good company.

Ana and Rosa Elena went to meet her at the station with a sign the little girl had made, in coloured letters: “Welcome, doña Remedios, the lamp lady.” Doña Remedios read it, laughed and asked Rosa Elena whether she had drawn the lamp herself. Rosa Elena said yes, and that she had copied it from a photo Andrei had shown her. Doña Remedios told her it had come out better than the soldier’s, and the soldier had drawn it at twenty. Rosa Elena answered, very proudly, that she was six. From that moment on, they were inseparable.

That night, Marta and Andrei organised a dinner in the flat on the calle del Prado. Doña Remedios walked slowly along the hallway, leaning on her stick, until she reached the green sign. She stood looking at it for a long time. Then she took some glasses out of her bag, put them on and read aloud: “Librería La Lámpara”. She said the soldier had promised her that sign in 1958, and that at last she was seeing it. Marta asked whether she wanted to touch it. Doña Remedios said there was no need; some things are better touched with the eyes.

Ecaterina gave her back the 1958 bookmark after dessert, in front of everyone, in the same envelope. Andrei also gave her a framed copy, printed large, to hang in the bookshop in Triana. Doña Remedios looked at both, the original and the copy, and said she would hang the copy on the wall and keep the original in the drawer, where it had been for sixty-eight years, because some things get used to their place. Curro, her grandson, took out his guitar and played something very softly. Nobody spoke for a while.

Before going to bed, doña Remedios asked Marta to show her the rest of the flat. Marta showed her the living room, the kitchen, Andrei’s room and, finally, her grandfather’s bedroom, which she had left almost as it was. Doña Remedios stood in the doorway without going in. She saw the bed, the bedside table, the wardrobe where Pilar had found the Romanian books. She asked Marta whether her grandfather had been happy at the end. Marta thought for a moment and said yes, the last year had been the best in many years. Doña Remedios nodded and said that was what she had come to find out.

On Saturday morning, at eleven, stall 112 already had a queue. Inés had placed two chairs behind the counter: one for Ecaterina and one for doña Remedios, who hadn’t written any book but appeared in the acknowledgements of the second edition, and had decided to sign there, under her name. Readers didn’t quite understand who that eighty-four-year-old lady with a fan was. When it was explained to them, they were stunned and asked her to sign for them too.

Doña Remedios’s signatures were very special. She wrote with an old fountain pen, slowly, in beautiful convent-school handwriting, and under each signature she drew a small lamp, just like the one on the bookmark. Readers stared at it as if it were a relic. A girl asked whether she could take her photo. Doña Remedios said yes, but not to put it on social media, because at her age she was too old to be famous. The girl posted it anyway. By the afternoon, the photo had ten thousand likes, and doña Remedios never found out.

At twelve, Faustino appeared. He had closed his stall on the Cuesta de Moyano for the second time in his life, and was wearing his special-occasions beret, the blue velvet one. He had heard about the bookseller from Triana and wanted to meet her. He planted himself in front of stall 112, looked her up and down and told her he had been told she didn’t mince her words. Doña Remedios closed her fan, looked him up and down in turn and replied that she had been told he talked nineteen to the dozen, and she could see they had hit the nail on the head.

Ecaterina asked Faustino not to pull her leg, because doña Remedios hadn’t slept a wink all night. Doña Remedios admitted she was worn out, but that there, among books, she was in her element. Faustino asked her whether the story about the bookmark was true. She said yes. He told her he had known Gil for forty years and that he used to steal his customers. She replied that he never bought anything from her, that he read for free on the floor, but that now he had sent her an author, and they were even.

From that moment on, Faustino didn’t budge from the stall. He started helping Inés with the boxes, although nobody had asked him, explaining to everyone that for him carrying boxes was a piece of cake. He brought doña Remedios a glass of water, then a coffee, then a new fan from a neighbouring stall, although she already had one. At one o’clock, he asked her whether she would have lunch with him. Doña Remedios said only if it was on him. Faustino replied that today he intended to spare no expense. Ana and Marta looked at each other without saying anything.

Inés, who was watching everything from a corner of the stall, came over to Ecaterina and whispered that she didn’t know what was going on between those two, but it was selling everything. In two hours the hundred copies of the second edition she had brought had sold out. She had had to call the warehouse to send another hundred by taxi. Ecaterina replied that what was going on was very simple: two old bookshops had met, and when two old bookshops meet, books sell themselves.

Meanwhile, Ecaterina was signing. Her hand had healed completely, and she signed quickly, almost as before the accident. But she still listened to each reader, because she had learnt in April that the signature was the least of it. A young woman told her she had read the book in hospital, looking after her father, and that her father had died the week before. She asked her to sign the book for him. Ecaterina wrote: “For Lucía’s father, who had a daughter who read aloud.” The woman left crying, but smiling.

Rosa Elena, for her part, had settled on a stool beside the stall, with her camera and an exercise book. Ana had explained some of the idioms she heard Faustino and doña Remedios use, and she had decided to make a dictionary. She wrote it in Romanian, with drawings, and asked her mother to write the idiom in Spanish. On one page she had drawn Faustino with enormous elbows. On another, Ecaterina lying on the floor, worn out, with a broom beside her. Faustino saw the elbows drawing and said the girl had hit the nail on the head.

At two, Costel and Señor Dan arrived, straight from the airport. They had come to Madrid, according to them, “for study purposes”: the C1 exam was in July, and they wanted to practise with real speakers. In fact they had come for the anniversary. Costel stood looking at stall 112, the queue, doña Remedios signing with her fan, Faustino carrying boxes. He told Señor Dan that a year earlier, in that very park, he had cried in front of a hundred people. Señor Dan replied that there was no need to remind him, because he was about to do it again.

And he did. But this time he didn’t cry from emotion, but because he put his foot in it. When he saw doña Remedios, he asked her out loud, with the best of intentions, whether she was Faustino’s mother. There was a terrible silence at the stall. Faustino went as red as a tomato. Doña Remedios closed her fan very slowly and told Costel that she was eighty-four, that Faustino was eighty-seven and that, if he wanted to pull his socks up for the C1, he would do well to learn to work out ages. Then she burst out laughing, and everyone laughed with her. Costel, from embarrassment, cried as well.

Andrei arrived at the stall at three, with his camera and some news. Begoña had called him that morning to tell him that a Barcelona magazine wanted to publish a six-page feature on “La lámpara encendida”, with his photos: the lamp at night, the empty drawer, Ecaterina signing with her good hand. They would pay him more than three months’ salary. Andrei told Ecaterina quietly. Ecaterina told him to tell his father before anyone else. Andrei called her first, even though she was standing in front of him. Then he called his father.

In the afternoon, when the signing was over, they all walked to the lake in the Retiro. Ecaterina wanted to see the bench, the Machado one, from May the year before. They found it occupied by a young couple kissing and paying no attention to anyone. Ecaterina stood looking at them from a distance for a moment. Then she told Ana there was no need to sit down; the bench was exactly as it should be. Rosa Elena took a photo of the young couple without them noticing. She said it was for the dictionary, for an idiom she didn’t know yet.

On the lake, Faustino hired a boat. Nobody understood why, not even him. He said he had been working two hundred metres from that lake for sixty years and had never been in a boat. He asked doña Remedios whether she wanted to get in with him. She told him she couldn’t swim. He told her neither could he. They both got in, very slowly, with help from Curro and Andrei, and Faustino rowed in circles for ten minutes, because he didn’t know how to row, while doña Remedios fanned herself and gave him instructions he didn’t follow. From the bank, everyone was taking photos.

Marta watched them with a notebook in her hand, jotting things down. Ecaterina asked her what she was writing. Marta said nothing, just some notes for the novel. Ecaterina asked whether the novel was going to have a happy ending, as doña Remedios had asked. Marta looked at the two old people in the boat, who at that moment were arguing about which way the bank was, and said that, from what she could see, she wouldn’t have much choice. Ecaterina laughed. She told her that, in her experience, happy endings wrote themselves, as long as someone left the door open.

Curro, the grandson, came over to Ecaterina on the bank while his grandmother went round in circles in the boat. He told her his grandmother hadn’t laughed like that for years, not since his grandfather died in 2009, and that in Triana nobody was going to believe what he was seeing. He asked her, very worried, what he should tell his mother when she called. Ecaterina advised him to tell her the truth: that his grandmother was in her element and that, for once, someone else was holding the oars. Curro laughed and said that, seeing how Faustino rowed, that wasn’t exactly a comfort.

That night they all had dinner at El Mostrador, which Lola had closed to the public for the occasion. There were sixteen of them. Carmen and Juan had brought tortilla. Lola had made croquetas. Pilar had come from Seville with her husband and a box of sweets from a convent. Mrs Florica, from Bucharest, had sent a jar of zacuscă with Costel and a note that said: “Don’t let the Spaniards eat it all.” Begoña didn’t come, but sent a bottle of wine with Lucas and a card with two words: “Not bad.”

During dinner, Ecaterina noticed that Faustino and doña Remedios had sat together without anyone arranging it, and were arguing quietly about whether Machado was better than Lorca. He defended Machado; she, Lorca, because he was Andalusian. Neither gave way. In the end, Faustino recited a Machado poem from memory, and doña Remedios, without letting him finish, answered with one by Lorca. The whole table fell silent, listening to them. Rosa Elena whispered to Ana whether it was a fight. Ana told her no, it was the opposite.

At ten, Lola switched off all the lights except the lamp at the back. Underneath, on the shelf, was still the first copy of the book, the “At last, delivered” one. Lola said that in the month it had been there, nobody had touched it, although many customers came over to look at it. Doña Remedios got up, went to the shelf leaning on her stick and stood looking at the book. Then she took out of her bag the original 1958 bookmark, the one she had said she would keep in the drawer, and slipped it inside the book, at the first page, without saying anything.

Ecaterina came over and asked whether she was sure. Doña Remedios replied that she had kept that bookmark for sixty-eight years waiting for an ending, and now that she knew it, the bookmark had to be where the ending was. That she had Andrei’s copy in Triana, and that was enough for her. “Besides,” she said, glancing sideways at Faustino, “at my age you have to make room in your drawers for new things.” Faustino went red again. Curro played the guitar. And the lamp, for the first time in a long while, lit up two bookmarks instead of one.

Before they left, very late, Costel asked to say something. Everyone fell silent, because Costel never asked to say anything. He took a crumpled piece of paper out of his pocket and read, in almost perfect Spanish, a short speech he had prepared on the plane. He said that a year earlier he was a lorry driver who cried in Hungary, and now he was a lorry driver who cried in Madrid, with a B2 and a C1 in July, which, in his opinion, was considerable progress. Everyone clapped. Doña Remedios said that man didn’t mince his words, and that, in a man, she liked that very much.

Faustino and doña Remedios were the last to leave. He offered to walk her to the hotel, which was two hundred metres away, and Curro discreetly hung back. Ecaterina watched them walk away along calle de las Huertas, slowly, each with a stick, arguing about something she couldn’t hear. When they reached the corner, Faustino took off his special-occasions beret, said something to doña Remedios, and she burst out laughing with her head thrown back. Ecaterina recognised that laugh. It was the same as in the 1985 photo.

Back at the flat on the calle del Prado, Rosa Elena asked Ana to write the last idiom of the day in the dictionary. Ana asked her which one. Rosa Elena showed her the photo she had taken at the lake: Faustino and doña Remedios in the boat, going round in circles, she with her fan, he with his oar the wrong way round. Ana thought for a moment and wrote underneath: “Estar en las nubes”. Rosa Elena asked what it meant. Ana told her it was what happened to grown-ups when they fell in love. Rosa Elena said that couldn’t be, because Faustino was eighty-seven. Ana replied that that was exactly why.
